items.title: Dave Frishberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001
items.q: Irving Berlin, Richard Rodgers, George Gershwin, that’s what changed jazz. ... the pop songwriters like even the unschooled ones were using the minor seventh like Irving Berlin.

ctx.x: Of the 20s, 30s, 40s, the golden, I mean Jerome Kern, Sigmund Romberg, Victor Herbert, Jerome Kern, Irving Berlin, Richard Rodgers, George Gershwin, that’s what changed jazz. That’s what opened the jazz musicians’ ears. That’s how jazz evolved. It was never referred to once in Ken Burns’ documentary by the way. Not once was that ever mentioned. The food of us jazz players, all of the jazz players, was the work of the greatest pop songwriters we’ve ever known and thank God we all, everybody coincided in the 1920s…

dramatic. You know what I mean? Where would Charlie Parker be if it weren’t for “All the Things You Are” and Jerome Kern, who defined the chordal movement of bebop with that song. That whole song is about bebop and where bebop went. The way he manipulated harmonies and then melody, and the way he harmonized that whole thing opened up jazz musicians’ ears all over the place, including a genius or two like Charlie Parker or Lester Young. The minor seventh is what changed jazz, okay?
